content: Frank Pantridge pioneered the development of the world’s first mobile coronary care unit (MCCU). He staffed this unit with an ambulance driver, a physician, and a nurse. However, the creation of the MCCU was not without challenges. Pantridge faced significant opposition, including skepticism from his cardiology colleagues and resistance from hospital staff. He noted that many of his non-cardiology medical colleagues were entirely unconvinced and uncooperative, as it was considered unconventional, if not outright illegal, to send junior hospital personnel, such as doctors and nurses, outside the hospital to provide care. Despite these obstacles, Pantridge’s MCCU program began operations on January 1, 1966. John Geddes, a cardiology resident at the Royal Victoria Hospital in Belfast, was part of Pantridge’s team. Geddes, along with four other residents, was responsible for accompanying the ambulance when it was dispatched. Geddes attributed the success of the program to two key factors: Pantridge’s remarkable and persuasive personality, which inspired enthusiasm and cooperation, and the hospital’s flat layout, which allowed for rapid access to patients and efficient resuscitation efforts. Geddes later observed that other hospitals in England, with slower elevators and less efficient designs, could not match the speed and effectiveness of the Belfast system. The initial results of the MCCU program were published in The Lancet on August 5, 1967, covering data from 312 patients over a 15-month period. Half of these patients had myocardial infarctions (MIs), and there were no deaths during transportation. Of particular significance were the outcomes of 10 patients who experienced cardiac arrest, all of whom had ventricular fibrillation. Six arrests occurred after the MCCU arrived, and four occurred shortly before its arrival. All 10 patients were successfully resuscitated and admitted to the hospital, with five eventually discharged alive. This publication had a profound impact, stimulating the development of prehospital emergency cardiac care programs worldwide. Historically, the MCCU program in Belfast marked a pivotal moment in resuscitation efforts. It represented the culmination of advancements in resuscitation techniques, including mouth-to-mouth ventilation, chest compressions, and portable defibrillation. Without these foundational elements, the program would not have succeeded. The Belfast system was designed to address acute myocardial infarction, with resuscitation efforts focused on patients whose hearts fibrillated after the ambulance arrived or en route. However, the system was less effective for patients who fibrillated before the call for help was made. The international readership of The Lancet facilitated the rapid dissemination of Pantridge’s ideas. Within two years, similar physician-staffed MCCU programs were established in Australia and Europe. In the United States, the first program was launched in 1968 by William Grace at St. Vincent’s Hospital in New York City. This program mirrored the Belfast model, utilizing specially equipped ambulances with physicians on board to provide advanced resuscitation care at the scene of cardiac emergencies. Calls involving chest pain were relayed from police 911 operators to the hospital, where a team of medical personnel—including physicians, nurses, and technicians—was dispatched. The team had a strict 4.5-minute deadline to assemble and board the ambulance, which typically reached the scene within 14 minutes. Grace’s program treated its first 161 patients, including three with ventricular fibrillation, one of whom survived. While innovative, the program was limited in scope and not nationally scalable. It highlighted the need for an evolution in prehospital emergency care, particularly in expanding resuscitation capabilities beyond physicians. This shift led to the development of paramedic-staffed units in communities such as Miami, Seattle, Portland, Los Angeles, and Columbus. These programs represented a significant advancement, focusing on sudden cardiac arrest as a primary concern rather than solely addressing myocardial infarction. Pantridge’s original program aimed to rapidly reach MI victims to reduce mortality during the critical early stages of the event. Consequently, cardiac arrest was successfully treated only if it occurred as a complication of MI and if the ambulance was already at the scene or en route. The transition to paramedic-staffed units marked a critical step in making resuscitation efforts more accessible and effective on a broader scale.
